allPracticeChanges.topic: PICO 5a In adult patients with aSAH and clinical deterioration due to delayed cerebral ischaemia, does hypertension induction compared to no hypertension induction decrease the risk of poor functional outcome?
allPracticeChanges.currentText: In adult patients with aSAH and clinical deterioration due to delayed cerebral ischaemia, no recommendation can be made on hypertension induction to decrease the risk of poor functional outcome.
allPracticeChanges.currentGrade: GRADE Uncertain / Ongoing trials (Evidence: Low, Voting: Vote: 11/13)
allPracticeChanges.picoQuestion: In adult patients with aSAH and clinical deterioration due to delayed cerebral ischaemia, does hypertension induction compared to no hypertension induction decrease the risk of poor functional outcome?
allPracticeChanges.expertConsensusStatement: In adult patients with aSAH and clinical deterioration due to delayed cerebral ischaemia, we suggest considering induced hypertension, provided that the ruptured aneurysm is treated and after standard therapy has proven insufficient. Clinical contraindications and potential complications of induced hypertension should be considered. (Vote: 11/13)

allPracticeChanges.topic: PICO 5b In adult patients with aSAH and clinical deterioration due to delayed cerebral ischaemia, does endovascular treatment of vasospasm compared to no endovascular treatment decrease the risk of poor functional outcome?
allPracticeChanges.currentText: In adult patients with aSAH and clinical deterioration due to delayed cerebral ischaemia, no recommendation can be made on endovascular treatment of vasospasm to decrease the risk of poor functional outcome.
allPracticeChanges.currentGrade: GRADE Uncertain / Ongoing trials (Evidence: Low, Voting: Vote: 13/13)
allPracticeChanges.picoQuestion: In adult patients with aSAH and clinical deterioration due to delayed cerebral ischaemia, does endovascular treatment of vasospasm compared to no endovascular treatment decrease the risk of poor functional outcome?
allPracticeChanges.expertConsensusStatement:
1. In adult patients with aSAH and clinical deterioration due to delayed cerebral ischaemia in combination with refractory and severe vasospasm, we suggest considering intra-arterial pharmacological treatment as a rescue therapy in selected patients to decrease the risk of poor functional outcome. (Vote: 11/13)
2. In adult patients with aSAH and clinical deterioration due to delayed cerebral ischaemia in combination with refractory severe vasospasm, the current evidence is insufficient to support the routine use of mechanical vasodilatation with balloon angioplasty. In selected cases, this approach may be considered as a last-line rescue treatment after careful multidisciplinary discussion of the potential risks and uncertain benefits. (Vote: 12/13)
3. In adult patients with aSAH and clinical deterioration due to delayed cerebral ischaemia in combination with refractory severe vasospasm, the current data are insufficient to support the use of mechanical vasodilatation with temporary deployment of retrievable stents to decrease the risk of poor functional outcome. (Vote: 13/13)

allPracticeChanges.topic: PICO 6a In adult patients with aSAH, does any type of neuroimaging compared to regular neurological examination decrease the risk of poor functional outcome?
allPracticeChanges.currentText: In adult patients with aSAH, no recommendation can be made on neuroimaging to decrease the risk of poor functional outcome.
allPracticeChanges.currentGrade: GRADE Uncertain / Ongoing trials (Evidence: Very low, Voting: Vote: 13/13)
allPracticeChanges.picoQuestion: In adult patients with aSAH, does any type of neuroimaging compared to regular neurological examination decrease the risk of poor functional outcome?
allPracticeChanges.expertConsensusStatement:
1. In adult patients with aSAH and clinical deterioration, we suggest plain head CT in combination with CT-Perfusion (CTP) imaging to detect the cause of deterioration. (Vote: 11/13)
2. In adult patients with aSAH who are neurologically not assessable but at high risk for DCI, we suggest plain head CT and CTP at least once between day 4 and 14. (Vote: 10/13)
3. In adult patients with aSAH, we do not suggest a routine DSA for screening of macrovascular vasospasm. (Vote: 13/13)

allPracticeChanges.topic: PICO 6b In adult patients with aSAH, does any type of neuromonitoring compared to regular neurological examination decrease the risk of poor functional outcome?
allPracticeChanges.currentText: In adult patients with aSAH, no recommendation can be made on neuromonitoring to decrease the risk of poor functional outcome.
allPracticeChanges.currentGrade: GRADE Uncertain / Ongoing trials (Evidence: Very low, Voting: Vote: 13/13)
allPracticeChanges.picoQuestion: In adult patients with aSAH, does any type of neuromonitoring compared to regular neurological examination decrease the risk of poor functional outcome?
allPracticeChanges.expertConsensusStatement:
1. In adult patients with aSAH, no suggestion can be given on the use of TCD monitoring. (Vote: 10/13)
2. In adult patients with aSAH and radiological hydrocephalus who are neurologically not assessable, we suggest ICP monitoring via EVD if an EVD is in place. (Vote: 13/13)
3. In adult patients with aSAH without radiological hydrocephalus who are neurologically not assessable, no suggestion can be given on ICP monitoring. (Vote: 11/13)
4. In adult patients with aSAH who are neurologically not assessable, we do not suggest invasive multimodal neuromonitoring with continuous measurement of partial pressure of brain tissue oxygen (PbtO2) and/or microdialysis due to the uncertain risk/benefit ratio of these modalities. (Vote: 10/13)
5. In adult patients with aSAH who are neurologically not assessable, we do not suggest the routine use of continuous EEG monitoring. (Vote: 13/13)

allPracticeChanges.topic: PICO 7 In adult patients with aSAH, does treatment of hydrocephalus (either by EVD, VP-shunt or lumbar drainage) compared to no treatment of hydrocephalus decrease the risk of poor functional outcome?
allPracticeChanges.currentText: In adult patients with aSAH and hydrocephalus, no recommendation can be made on CSF diversion strategies to decrease the risk of poor functional outcome.
allPracticeChanges.currentGrade: GRADE Uncertain / Ongoing trials (Evidence: Very low, Voting: Vote: 13/13)
allPracticeChanges.picoQuestion: In adult patients with aSAH, does treatment of hydrocephalus (either by EVD, VP-shunt or lumbar drainage) compared to no treatment of hydrocephalus decrease the risk of poor functional outcome?
allPracticeChanges.expertConsensusStatement:
1. In adult patients with aSAH who present with radiological hydrocephalus and a decreased level of consciousness, we suggest CSF drainage. (Vote: 13/13)
2. In adult patients with aSAH who present with obstructive hydrocephalus and a decreased level of consciousness, we suggest EVD placement. (Vote: 13/13)
3. In adult patients with aSAH who present with communicating hydrocephalus and a decreased level of consciousness, we suggest LD or repeated LPs as the strategy of first choice for CSF drainage. (Vote: 11/13)
4. In adult patients with aSAH who present with radiological hydrocephalus and a normal level of consciousness, we do not suggest CSF drainage. (Vote: 12/13)
5. In adult patients with aSAH who come at a point at which prolonged CSF drainage (by EVD, LD or repeated LPs) carries a higher risk of severe complications than placement of a permanent CSF diversion, we suggest permanent CSF diversion. (Vote: 13/13)
6. In adult patients with aSAH who present with symptomatic chronic hydrocephalus, we suggest permanent CSF diversion. (Vote: 13/13)

allPracticeChanges.topic: PICO 8 In adult patients with aSAH, does treatment on a dedicated neuro-ICU or high care unit compared to a general ICU or high care unit decrease the risk of poor functional outcome?
allPracticeChanges.currentText: In adult patients with aSAH, no recommendation can be made on admission to a dedicated neuro-ICU or high care unit to decrease the risk of poor functional outcome.
allPracticeChanges.currentGrade: GRADE Uncertain / Ongoing trials (Evidence: Very low, Voting: Vote: 13/13)
allPracticeChanges.picoQuestion: In adult patients with aSAH, does treatment on a dedicated neuro-ICU or high care unit compared to a general ICU or high care unit decrease the risk of poor functional outcome?
allPracticeChanges.expertConsensusStatement: In adult patients with aSAH, we suggest admission and management in a dedicated neuro-ICU or high care unit to decrease the risk of poor functional outcome. (Vote: 13/13)

allPracticeChanges.topic: PICO 9a In adult patients with aSAH, does treatment in a high-volume centre compared to a low-volume centre decrease the risk of poor functional outcome?
allPracticeChanges.currentText: In adult patients with aSAH, no recommendation can be made on admission/transfer to a high-volume centre to decrease the risk of poor functional outcome.
allPracticeChanges.currentGrade: GRADE Uncertain / Ongoing trials (Evidence: Very low, Voting: Vote: 12/13)
allPracticeChanges.picoQuestion: In adult patients with aSAH, does treatment in a high-volume centre compared to a low-volume centre decrease the risk of poor functional outcome?
allPracticeChanges.expertConsensusStatement: We suggest that all patients with spontaneous SAH are admitted or immediately transferred to centres that treat at least 70 patients with aSAH per year, or at least 35 patients with aSAH per year in remote areas where access is limited. (Vote: 12/13)

allPracticeChanges.topic: PICO 9b In adult patients with aSAH, does aneurysm treatment by a high-volume neurosurgeon or neurointerventionalist compared to a low-volume neurosurgeon or neurointerventionalist decrease the risk of poor functional outcome?
allPracticeChanges.currentText: In adult patients with aSAH, no recommendation can be made on case-volume per neurosurgeon and neurointerventionalist to decrease the risk of poor functional outcome.
allPracticeChanges.currentGrade: GRADE Uncertain / Ongoing trials (Evidence: Very low, Voting: Vote: 12/13)
allPracticeChanges.picoQuestion: In adult patients with aSAH, does aneurysm treatment by a high-volume neurosurgeon or neurointerventionalist compared to a low-volume neurosurgeon or neurointerventionalist decrease the risk of poor functional outcome?
allPracticeChanges.expertConsensusStatement: In adult patients with aSAH, we suggest that aneurysms are repaired by neurosurgeons or neurointerventionalists who perform the treatment of choice in more than 30 patients with aneurysms (ruptured and unruptured) per year. (Vote: 12/13)

allPracticeChanges.topic: PICO 10 In adult patients with aSAH, does a radiological follow-up beyond 6 months after aneurysm treatment compared to a maximum radiological follow-up duration of 6 months decrease the risk of poor functional outcome?
allPracticeChanges.currentText: In adult patients with aSAH, no recommendation can be made on radiological follow-up beyond 6 months after microsurgical or endovascular aneurysm treatment to decrease the risk of poor functional outcome.
allPracticeChanges.currentGrade: GRADE Uncertain / Ongoing trials (Evidence: Very low, Voting: Vote: 13/13)
allPracticeChanges.picoQuestion: In adult patients with aSAH, does a radiological follow-up beyond 6 months after aneurysm treatment compared to a maximum radiological follow-up duration of 6 months decrease the risk of poor functional outcome?
allPracticeChanges.expertConsensusStatement:
1. In adult patients with aSAH who are treated with coils and adequate occlusion within 6 months, we suggest at least one additional radiological follow-up at or beyond 12 months after aneurysm repair to investigate potential aneurysm recanalization, as long as a potential re-treatment remains an option. (Vote: 13/13)
2. In adult patients with aSAH who were treated with clip reconstruction and adequate occlusion within 6 months, we do not suggest further radiological follow-up to investigate potential aneurysm recanalization. (Vote: 11/13)
3. In adult patients with aSAH who have neck remnants or partially occluded aneurysms (irrespective of type of aneurysm treatment), we suggest radiological follow-up beyond 6 months after aneurysm treatment as long as a potential re-treatment remains an option. (Vote: 13/13)
4. In adult patients with aSAH who are treated with endovascular devices other than coils, we suggest radiological follow-up at least five years after treatment, regardless of the degree of occlusion, to ensure adequate long-term occlusion and as long as a potential re-treatment remains an option. (Vote: 11/13)
5. In adult patients with aSAH, we suggest radiological follow-up beyond 6 months after aneurysm treatment in order to evaluate for de novo aneurysms at 5-year intervals as long as a potential treatment remains an option, in those with a high-risk profile (such as young age, positive family history for aSAH, autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease). (Vote: 12/13)

allPracticeChanges.topic: PICO 1: In hospitalised adults with acute ischaemic or haemorrhagic stroke (non-ventilated) within 7 days of stroke symptom onset, does use of any standardised diagnostic criteria for SAP, compared to non-standardised clinician-based diagnosis, improve clinical outcomes?
allPracticeChanges.category: In hospitalised adults with acute ischaemic or haemorrhagic
allPracticeChanges.currentText: In hospitalised adults with acute ischaemic or haemorrhagic stroke (non-ventilated) within 7 days of stroke symptom onset, there are insufficient data to support recommendations on whether the use of standardised diagnostic criteria for SAP improves clinical outcomes. Consequently, no evidence-based recommendation can be made. Please see the Expert Consensus Statement below.
allPracticeChanges.currentGrade: GRADE Uncertain / Ongoing trials (Evidence: Uncertain / Ongoing trial, Voting: Vote: 8/8)
allPracticeChanges.picoQuestion: In hospitalised adults with acute ischaemic or haemorrhagic stroke (non-ventilated) within 7 days of stroke symptom onset, does use of any standardised diagnostic criteria for SAP, compared to non-standardised clinician-based diagnosis, improve clinical outcomes?
allPracticeChanges.expertConsensusStatement: In the absence of appropriately designed RCTs, and on the basis of observational studies and secondary analysis of RCTs, we suggest to use an algorithm-based approach for SAP diagnosis (for example PISCES) guided by a minimum set of agreed criteria. This may improve diagnostic accuracy and require further evaluation in research in clinical practice.

allPracticeChanges.topic: PICO 2: In hospitalised adults with acute ischaemic or haemorrhagic stroke (non-ventilated) within 7 days of stroke symptom onset, does use of chest ultrasound or computed tomography to diagnose SAP, compared to chest X-ray alone, increase diagnostic accuracy and improve clinical outcomes?
allPracticeChanges.category: In hospitalised adults with acute ischaemic or haemorrhagic
allPracticeChanges.currentText: In hospitalised adults with acute ischaemic or haemorrhagic stroke (non-ventilated) within 7 days of stroke symptom onset, uncertainty remains regarding the most accurate diagnostic approach for SAP when using chest ultrasound or computed tomography compared with chest X-ray alone. The potential benefits and risks of these procedures in relation to clinical outcomes are also unclear. Therefore, no evidence-based recommendation can currently be made. Please see the Expert Consensus Statement below.
allPracticeChanges.currentGrade: GRADE Uncertain / Ongoing trials (Evidence: Uncertain / Ongoing trial, Voting: Vote: 8/8)
allPracticeChanges.picoQuestion: In hospitalised adults with acute ischaemic or haemorrhagic stroke (non-ventilated) within 7 days of stroke symptom onset, does use of chest ultrasound or computed tomography to diagnose SAP, compared to chest X-ray alone, increase diagnostic accuracy and improve clinical outcomes?
allPracticeChanges.expertConsensusStatement: We suggest to consider a pulmonary CT scan if SAP is suspected and the diagnosis uncertain, particularly where there is a need to inform further antibiotic/ medical therapy and/or exclude other pathologies (e.g. pulmonary embolism).

allPracticeChanges.topic: PICO 4: In hospitalised adults with acute ischaemic or haemorrhagic stroke (non-ventilated) within 7 days of stroke symptom onset, does use of clinical prediction scores or biomarkers, compared to not using clinical prediction scores or biomarkers, identify patients who will develop SAP?
allPracticeChanges.category: In hospitalised adults with acute ischaemic or haemorrhagic
allPracticeChanges.currentText: In hospitalised adults with acute ischaemic or haemorrhagic stroke (non-ventilated) within 7 days of stroke symptom onset, clinical prediction scores and selected biomarkers may help identify individuals at increased risk of developing SAP, with moderate to good discriminatory performance. However, there is currently insufficient evidence to support the routine combination of biomarkers with existing clinical prediction tools for risk stratification. Continued uncertainty remains regarding the incremental clinical value of these approaches, and their implementation will ultimately depend on the availability, feasibility, and effectiveness of targeted preventive interventions. Please refer to the Expert Consensus Statement below.
allPracticeChanges.currentGrade: GRADE Weak for intervention (Evidence: Very low, Voting: Vote: 8/8)
allPracticeChanges.picoQuestion: In hospitalised adults with acute ischaemic or haemorrhagic stroke (non-ventilated) within 7 days of stroke symptom onset, does use of clinical prediction scores or biomarkers, compared to not using clinical prediction scores or biomarkers, identify patients who will develop SAP?
allPracticeChanges.expertConsensusStatement: We suggest using validated clinical prediction scores or biomarkers to identify patients at increased risk of SAP and to better target preventive standard measures. However, their clinical utility is currently limited by only moderate to good discriminatory performance and is likely to depend on the availability of more effective preventive treatment strategies.

allPracticeChanges.expertConsensusStatement: Other preventive treatments: In hospitalised, non-ventilated adults with acute ischaemic or haemorrhagic stroke within 7 days of symptom onset, concomitant medications prescribed for other indications may influence the risk of SAP. Acid-suppressive therapy may increase SAP risk, whereas treatment with ACEIs or ARBs in patients with intracerebral haemorrhage may be associated with reduced pneumonia and mortality risk. Given the limited evidence, we suggest considering these potential effects and using these medications strictly according to their primary indications, i.e. PPIs/H2 antagonists for the prevention and treatment of peptic ulceration, and ACEIs or ARBs for the management of hypertension.

allPracticeChanges.expertConsensusStatement: Based on the results of a single small study (turn-mob) we suggest that patients, including those with reduced level of consciousness, should be turned from supine to the left and right lateral recumbent position every 2 hours during the day and mobilized passively in bed to prevent SAP, if they are unable to change position independently. In line with clinical practice and guidance for enteral feeding, we suggest that during and after enteral feeds patients should be nursed in the 30-45 degree head-up position to avoid aspiration. Guided by the results of the HeadPost study, we suggest that alert patients with mild strokes and without enteral tubes in place should maintain any position they find comfortable.

allPracticeChanges.currentText: In individuals 40-79 years of age, estimation of risk for atherosclerotic CVD (ie, nonfatal MI, nonfatal stroke, and fatal CVD) every 1 to 5 years is beneficial to guide decisions on treatments and lifestyle recommendations that may reduce risk for stroke.
In individuals with AF, calculation of the CHA2DS2-VASc score is recommended to guide decisions on prescription of oral anticoagulation to reduce risk for stroke.
In individuals >=18 years of age, periodic screening for modifiable behaviors and medical conditions that increase stroke risk is recommended to reduce risk for stroke.
In individuals >=18 years of age, periodic screening for SDOH (eg, food insecurity, lack of transportation) is beneficial to identify additional factors that contribute to stroke risk.
In adults without prior CVD and who are at high or intermediate CVD risk, a Mediterranean diet is recommended to reduce the risk of incident stroke.

In adults who are >=60 years of age and have uncontrolled BP (systolic BP [SBP] >=140 mm Hg if taking antihypertensive medication or >=160 mm Hg if not), compared with using 100% sodium chloride, salt substitution (75% sodium chloride and 25% potassium chloride) is reasonable to reduce the risk of incident stroke.
In adults, folic acid supplementation and B-complex (folic acid, B12, B6) vitamins supplementation for reducing the risk of stroke are not well established.
In adults without prior CVD, long-chain fatty acids are not effective for reducing the risk of stroke.
In adults, vitamin C, vitamin E, selenium, antioxidants, calcium, calcium with vitamin D, and multivitamin supplementation are not effective for reducing the risk of stroke.
In adults, screening for physical activity is recommended as part of a comprehensive effort to estimate stroke risk.

In adults, counseling patients to engage in at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity physical activity, 75 minutes of vigorous-intensity physical activity, or an equivalent combination per week is recommended to reduce the risk of stroke.

In adults, counseling to avoid excessive time spent in sedentary behavior (characterized by low-energy expenditure while sitting, reclining, or lying while awake) is recommended to reduce the risk of stroke.
In adults >18 years of age, screening for overweight and obesity is recommended to inform the risk of stroke.
In patients with class II obesity (35-39.9 kg/m2) or greater, bariatric surgical procedures to promote weight loss may be considered to reduce the risk of stroke.
The effectiveness of screening adults for OSA to prevent stroke is unclear.
In patients with OSA, continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) might be reasonable to reduce the risk of stroke.
In asymptomatic adults >=18 years of age who have overweight, obesity, or atherosclerotic CVD, screening for prediabetes and diabetes is recommended to inform stroke risk.
In patients with diabetes and high cardiovascular risk or established CVD and hemoglobin A1c >=7%, treatment with a GLP-1 receptor agonist is effective to reduce the risk of stroke.
In patients with type 1 diabetes or diabetes, intensive glycemic control (targeting a hemoglobin A1c <=6.5%) is not beneficial for stroke prevention.
In adults >=18 years of age, screening for hypertension is recommended to identify individuals at increased risk for stroke and eligible for antihypertensive treatment.

In adults with stage 2 hypertension or stage 1 hypertension with a higher risk for atherosclerotic CVD, lifestyle improvement and antihypertensive drug treatment to a SBP/diastolic BP (DBP) <130/80 mm Hg are recommended to prevent stroke.

In adults with hypertension, thiazide and thiazide-like diuretics, calcium channel blockers, angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, and angiotensin receptor blockers are recommended as initial antihypertensive drug therapies to prevent stroke.
In most adults with hypertension, antihypertensive drug treatment incorporating >=2 antihypertensive medications is indicated to achieve the BP control necessary to prevent stroke.

In adults who qualify for treatment with lipid-lowering therapy according to the 2019 ACC/AHA guideline on the primary prevention of CVD (eg, 20-75 years of age with LDL cholesterol [LDL-C] level >190 mg/dL [>4.9 mmol/L], 10-year ASCVD risk >=20%, or 10-year ASCVD risk >=7.5%-<20% plus >=1 risk enhancers), treatment with a statin is recommended to reduce the risk of a first stroke.

In adults without CVD who qualify for treatment with lipid-lowering therapy, according to the 2019 ACC/AHA guideline on the primary prevention of CVD (eg, 20-75 years of age with LDL-C level >190 mg/dL [>4.9 mmol/L], 10-year ASCVD risk >=20%, or 10-year ASCVD risk >=7.5%-<20% plus >=1 risk enhancers), who cannot reach goals or cannot tolerate other therapies such as statins, the benefit of treatment with alirocumab or evolocumab compared with other active lipid-lowering therapy for the reduction of the risk of a first stroke is uncertain.

In adults who do not tolerate statin therapy and who have LDL-C >100 mg/dL and elevated cardiovascular risk, treatment with bempedoic acid to reduce the risk of a first stroke is not well established.
In adults with moderate or low intake of long-chain omega-3 fatty acid, supplementation is not recommended to reduce the risk of a first stroke.

In all patients, screening for cigarette smoking, use of other forms of tobacco, use of electronic nicotine delivery systems such as electronic cigarettes (e-cigarettes) and vapes, and environmental tobacco smoke exposure (secondhand smoke exposure) is effective to inform stroke risk and target cessation interventions.

For patients who are nonusers of tobacco products, continued complete abstention from cigarette smoking, in addition to other tobacco products and electronic nicotine delivery systems, and avoidance of exposure to environmental tobacco smoke (secondhand smoke exposure) are recommended to avoid the associated increased risk of stroke.

For patients who are active cigarette smokers, smoking cessation pharmacotherapy delivered along with behavioral counseling is recommended, in preference to behavioral counseling alone, to facilitate smoking cessation.

allPracticeChanges.topic: Cessation Support for Other Tobacco Products
allPracticeChanges.currentText: For patients who are active cigarette smokers and users of other tobacco products (eg, electronic nicotine delivery systems), assistance with cessation is recommended to reduce the risk of stroke.

For patients who are active cigarette smokers encountered in the hospital setting, providing smoking cessation pharmacotherapy along with behavioral counseling as the default treatment ("opt-out"), in preference to providing such treatment only for patients expressing a willingness to quit smoking ("opt-in"), can be beneficial to facilitate short-term smoking cessation and to increase engagement in smoking cessation treatment.

For patients who are active cigarette smokers, the long-term health benefits of using e-cigarettes in place of nicotine replacement therapy to facilitate cigarette smoking cessation are not well established.
In the asymptomatic population, routine screening for carotid artery stenosis is not recommended to reduce the risk of stroke.

In patients with asymptomatic carotid artery stenosis (ACS) >70%, shared decision-making between the patient and the health care team to decide between the 2 courses of treatment (carotid revascularization or medical management) is recommended to determine the best method of reducing stroke risk.
In patients with asymptomatic atherosclerotic carotid artery stenosis, medical treatment with statin can be beneficial to reduce the risk of stroke.

allPracticeChanges.topic: Carotid Revascularization for Low Perioperative Risk ACS
allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with asymptomatic atherosclerotic carotid artery stenosis >70% and low perioperative risk, the use of carotid revascularization, in addition to intensive medical therapy, may be reasonable to reduce the risk of stroke.
In patients with ACS >50%, annual carotid duplex ultrasound every 6 to 12 months might be reasonable to assess progression of disease and subsequent increased risk of stroke.
In patients with asymptomatic atherosclerotic carotid artery stenosis and high perioperative risk, the effectiveness of carotid revascularization to reduce risk of stroke is not established.

In adults with asymptomatic cerebral SVD (CSVD), including silent infarcts, assessment and management of risk factors (eg, hypertension, dyslipidemia, tobacco use, and diabetes) are recommended to reduce stroke risk.

allPracticeChanges.topic: Statin Therapy for Silent Cerebral Infarcts
allPracticeChanges.currentText: In adults with silent cerebral infarcts (SCIs) who do not have an indication for statin therapy according to the 2019 ACC/AHA guideline (eg, 20-75 years of age with LDL-C level >190 mg/dL [>4.9 mmol/L], 10-year ASCVD risk >=20%, or 10-year ASCVD risk >=7.5%-<20% plus >=1 more risk enhancers), use of low-dose statin therapy might be considered to reduce the risk of ischemic stroke.
In adults with SCI, the benefit of antiplatelet therapy to reduce the risk of ischemic stroke is uncertain.

In adults 18 to 64 years of age with migraine with or without aura, evaluation and modification of vascular risk factors are recommended to address the elevated risk of stroke in this patient population.

In adults with migraine with aura who desire contraception, progestin-only or nonhormonal forms are recommended to avoid the increased risk of ischemic stroke associated with combined hormonal contraception.

In children 2 to 16 years of age with SCD (Hb SS or Hb S-beta0-thalassemia), transcranial Doppler (TCD) screening at a frequency based on the highest mean flow velocity in the terminal portion of the internal carotid or the proximal portion of the middle cerebral artery is recommended.

allPracticeChanges.topic: Transfusion Therapy for Elevated Stroke Risk in SCD
allPracticeChanges.currentText: In children 2 to 16 years of age with SCD at elevated risk per TCD measurements, regularly scheduled transfusion therapy (target reduction of hemoglobin S <30%) is effective for reducing stroke risk.

allPracticeChanges.topic: Brain MRI for Silent Infarcts in SCD
allPracticeChanges.currentText: In children 2 to 16 years of age and young adults with Hb SS or Hb S-beta0-thalassemia, an MRI of the brain without sedation should be performed as soon as possible to evaluate for SCI and to determine the need for chronic red cell transfusions (CRCTs) for stroke prevention.
In children 2 to 16 years of age with SCD whose TCD velocities revert to normal, continued transfusion therapy can be beneficial to reduce the risk of stroke.
In children 2 to 16 years of age with SCD and normalized mean flow velocities and no intracranial stenosis, transition from transfusion to hydroxyurea therapy can be considered to prevent stroke.

allPracticeChanges.topic: Hydroxyurea or BMT for High-Risk SCD Unable to Transfuse
allPracticeChanges.currentText: In children 2 to 16 years of age with SCD at high risk for stroke (TCD mean flow velocities >=200 cm/s) but without intracranial stenosis who are unable to continue or cannot be treated with periodic red cell transfusion, hydroxyurea or bone marrow transplantation may be reasonable to prevent stroke.
In patients with CADASIL, counseling on smoking cessation and treatment of hypertension and other vascular risk factors are beneficial to reduce the risk of incident stroke.

In adults with hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia (HHT), screening for pulmonary arteriovenous malformations (PAVMs) is reasonable to identify the need for multidisciplinary evaluation to manage stroke risk.

allPracticeChanges.topic: Enzyme Replacement Therapy in Fabry Disease
allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with Fabry disease, the effectiveness of enzyme replacement therapy (ERT) to reduce the risk of stroke is not well established.
In adults with a recent MI, the addition of low-dose colchicine to intensive statin therapy might be reasonable to decrease the risk of ischemic stroke.

In patients without a history of stroke and no clinical indication for anticoagulation, with a high-risk aPL profile (ie, triple-positive antiphospholipid testing [lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin antibody, anti-beta2 glycoprotein 1] or double-positive [any combination] or isolated lupus anticoagulant or isolated persistently positive anticardiolipin antibody at medium to high titers), prophylactic treatment with aspirin (75-100 mg daily) is recommended to reduce the risk of stroke.

allPracticeChanges.topic: Aspirin for SLE with High-Risk aPL
allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and no history of thrombosis or pregnancy complications and with a high-risk antiphospholipid profile (ie, lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin antibody, anti-beta2-glycoprotein 1, or double-positive [any combination] or isolated lupus anticoagulant or isolated persistently positive anticardiolipin antibody at medium to high titers), prophylactic treatment with aspirin (75-100 mg daily) is recommended to reduce the risk of stroke.

allPracticeChanges.topic: Anticoagulation in APS with Prior Venous Thrombosis
allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with antiphospholipid syndrome (APS) with prior unprovoked venous thrombosis, it is reasonable to choose vitamin K antagonist (VKA) therapy with a target international normalized ratio of 2 to 3 in preference to aspirin or direct oral anticoagulants for prevention of recurrent thrombotic events, including stroke.
In patients with rheumatoid arthritis, statin treatment may be reasonable to reduce major adverse cardiovascular events, including stroke.

In nonpregnant adults with a history of obstetric APS only, prophylactic treatment with aspirin (75-100 mg daily) after adequate risk/benefit evaluation (ie, aPL profile, coexistent traditional cardiovascular risk factors, intolerance, or contraindication to aspirin) may be considered to reduce the risk of stroke.

allPracticeChanges.topic: Aspirin for SLE with Low-Risk aPL
allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with SLE and no history of thrombosis or pregnancy complications and with a low-risk antiphospholipid profile (ie, isolated anticardiolipin antibody or anti-beta2-glycoprotein 1 antibodies at low to medium titers, particularly if transiently positive), prophylactic treatment with aspirin (75-100 mg daily) may be considered to reduce the risk of stroke.
In patients with periodontal disease (PD), good oral hygiene and regular dental care can be beneficial to lower stroke risk.
In patients hospitalized with COVID-19, treatment with full-dose anticoagulation (eg, enoxaparin, apixaban) is not recommended to prevent stroke.
In all adults, screening for substance misuse and substance use disorders (eg, alcohol, cannabis, cocaine, opioids, amphetamines) is recommended to inform stroke risk.

In patients who use recreational drugs (eg, cannabis, synthetic cannabinoids, cocaine, heroin, methamphetamine), misuse alcohol or prescription medications (eg, stimulants and opioids), or have a substance use disorder, counseling to stop or appropriate substance use disorder treatments (eg, pharmacological, behavioral, or multimodal) as appropriate are reasonable to reduce stroke risk.

In pregnant or early postpartum (within 6 weeks of delivery), patients with severe hypertension (2 measurements of SBP >=160 mm Hg or DBP >=110 mm Hg, 15 minutes apart), BP-lowering treatment to a target <160/110 mm Hg as soon as possible is recommended to reduce the risk of fatal maternal ICH.

allPracticeChanges.topic: Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy BP Control
allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with HDP, including chronic hypertension in pregnancy, treatment with antihypertensive medication to a goal BP of <140/90 mm Hg is reasonable to reduce the risk of pregnancy-associated stroke.

In adults, screening for a history of certain adverse pregnancy outcomes (APOs), including HDP, preterm birth, gestational diabetes, and placental disorders, followed by subsequent evaluation and management of vascular risk factors, is recommended to reduce the risk of stroke.
In patients with a history of HDP or other APOs, early evaluation and management of chronic hypertension are recommended to reduce the risk of stroke.
In adults, screening for a history of endometriosis is reasonable to inform the risk of stroke.
In individuals with endometriosis, vascular risk factor evaluation and modification of vascular risk factors are reasonable to reduce the risk of stroke.

allPracticeChanges.topic: Ethinyl Estradiol Dose Minimization in CHC
allPracticeChanges.currentText: In individuals considering CHC, lower doses of ethinyl estradiol are recommended to minimize potential increased stroke risk.

allPracticeChanges.topic: Contraception Shared Decision-Making in High-Risk Factors
allPracticeChanges.currentText: In individuals with specific stroke risk factors (ie, age >35 years, tobacco use, hypertension, or migraine with aura) who are considering contraception, shared decision-making is recommended to determine the best contraceptive choice to balance the risk of stroke from contraception and the risk of stroke with pregnancy.

allPracticeChanges.topic: Progestin-Only or Nonhormonal Contraception in High-Risk
allPracticeChanges.currentText: In individuals with specific stroke risk factors (ie, age >35 years, tobacco use, hypertension, or migraine with aura) who are considering contraception, progestin-only contraception or nonhormonal contraception is reasonable to prevent the increased stroke risk associated with estrogen-containing contraception.
Screening for a history of premature ovarian failure (before 40 years of age) and early menopause (before 45 years of age) can be beneficial to inform the risk of stroke.

allPracticeChanges.topic: Risk Factor Evaluation in Premature/Early Menopause
allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with premature ovarian failure (menopause before 40 years of age) or early menopause (before 45 years of age), evaluation and modification of vascular risk factors are recommended to reduce the elevated stroke risk in this population.

In women >=60 years of age, more than 10 years after natural menopause, or at elevated risk for CVD or stroke, oral estrogen-containing menopausal HT is associated with an excess risk of stroke and must be weighed against clinical benefits.
In transgender women and gender-diverse individuals taking estrogens for gender affirmation, evaluation and modification of risk factors can be beneficial to reduce the risk of stroke.

In men 45 to 80 years of age with confirmed hypogonadism who are considering testosterone therapy, initiation or continuation of testosterone replacement therapy is reasonable and does not increase the risk of stroke.

allPracticeChanges.topic: Anticoagulation in Left Ventricular Systolic Dysfunction
allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with left ventricular systolic dysfunction (ejection fraction <=35%-40%) and no evidence of AF or left ventricular thrombus, anticoagulation is not indicated to prevent stroke and is associated with a higher bleeding risk.

allPracticeChanges.topic: Aspirin for Diabetes or Vascular Risk Factors
allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with diabetes or other common vascular risk factors and no prior stroke, the use of aspirin to prevent a first stroke is not well established.

allPracticeChanges.topic: Ticagrelor in Stable Coronary Artery Disease
allPracticeChanges.currentText: In patients with established, stable coronary artery disease and a low bleeding risk, the addition of ticagrelor to aspirin beyond 12 months for a period up to 3 years may be beneficial to reduce the rate of ischemic stroke.
In individuals >=70 years of age with at least 1 additional cardiovascular risk factor, the use of aspirin is not beneficial to prevent a first stroke.
In patients with chronic kidney disease, the use of aspirin is not effective to prevent a first stroke.
